title: One DynamoDB partition: a client, a request router with its caches, and a replication group of three replicas in three Availability Zones
caption: Based on Elhemali et al., Amazon DynamoDB, USENIX ATC 2022. One partition is shown; real storage nodes host replicas of many partitions. Which replica serves an eventually consistent read, and where a log replica is placed, are illustrative: the paper doesn't say.

steps.title: A write arrives
steps.text: The app calls PutItem to change cart#42 from v1 to v2. Every request lands first on a request router, a fleet that sits in front of the storage nodes.

steps.title: Who is calling?
steps.text: The router authenticates the request with IAM, and with KMS for tables encrypted with customer keys. It answers from a cache that it refreshes in the background, so if IAM or KMS has an outage, routers keep using cached results for a set period. The paper calls this static stability.

steps.title: Which partition owns the key?
steps.text: The partition key is hashed, and each partition owns a contiguous slice of the hashed key range. The router's partition-map cache says which storage nodes host that partition. Even on a cache hit, the router refreshes the entry from MemDS in the background, so MemDS sees the same load whether router caches are warm or cold.

steps.title: Is there capacity?
steps.text: Admission control. The router spends a token from its local bucket for this table. Global admission control (GAC) refills that bucket every few seconds based on the whole table's consumption, so traffic aimed at a few items can still use up to a partition's maximum capacity. Per-partition token buckets remain as a cap.

steps.title: Send it to the leader
steps.text: The partition has three replicas in three Availability Zones, forming a replication group that runs Multi-Paxos. Only the leader accepts writes.

steps.title: Replicate the log record
steps.text: The leader generates a write-ahead log record for the change and sends it to both peers.

steps.title: Quorum
steps.text: AZ 2 persists the record in its own write-ahead log and replies. Two of three replicas is a write quorum, so the write can be acknowledged. The leader doesn't wait for AZ 3.

steps.title: Acknowledge
steps.text: The leader confirms the write and the router returns success to the app.

steps.title: Catch up and archive
steps.text: AZ 3 persists the record too. In the background, write-ahead logs are archived to S3 after checks on every entry's checksum and sequence number. That archive feeds backups, point-in-time restore over the last 35 days, and the scrub process that compares live replicas with a copy rebuilt from the log.

steps.title: A read that must be current
steps.text: The app calls GetItem with ConsistentRead set. At this moment AZ 3 hasn't applied the latest write yet: it still holds v1.

steps.title: Only the leader answers
steps.text: After the same authentication, routing and admission checks as a write, the router sends the read to the partition's leader. Only the leader serves strongly consistent reads, because every write goes through it.

steps.title: The latest value
steps.text: The app gets v2, the latest acknowledged value, even though AZ 3 is behind.

steps.title: The same read, relaxed
steps.text: The app calls GetItem without ConsistentRead. AZ 3 still holds v1.

steps.title: Any replica can answer
steps.text: Any replica in the group can serve an eventually consistent read, which spreads reads across all three. Suppose this one goes to AZ 3.

steps.title: A slightly old value
steps.text: AZ 3 hasn't applied the latest write, so the app gets v1. A moment later the same read would return v2. That's the trade: any replica can answer, but the answer may be slightly behind.

steps.title: A storage node dies
steps.text: The storage node holding the AZ 3 replica fails. The two remaining replicas are still a write quorum, but one more failure would stop writes to this partition.

steps.title: A full rebuild is slow
steps.text: Healing a storage replica means copying its B-tree and write-ahead log to a new node. That takes several minutes.

steps.title: Add a log replica instead
steps.text: The leader adds a log replica. It stores only recent write-ahead log entries, with no B-tree, so it's ready in a few seconds. Like an acceptor in Paxos, it counts towards the write quorum.

steps.title: Writes keep flowing
steps.text: New log records go to AZ 2 and the log replica. The log replica holds no key-value data, so it can't serve reads, but it keeps the partition writable and durable while a full replacement is built.

steps.title: Missed heartbeats
steps.text: AZ 3 stops hearing the leader's heartbeats. The leader is healthy; only the path between those two replicas is broken. This is a gray failure: some components see a problem and others don't.

steps.title: Ask before acting
steps.text: A new election would interrupt writes, so before starting one, AZ 3 asks the other replica whether it can still reach the leader.

steps.title: Stand down
steps.text: It can, so AZ 3 drops its attempt. No election, no interruption. The paper reports that this check significantly cut spurious leader elections.

steps.title: Now the leader really fails
steps.text: This time the leader's node dies. Writes and strongly consistent reads for this partition stop until there's a new leader. Eventually consistent reads can still go to AZ 2 or AZ 3.

steps.title: Elect a new leader
steps.text: The surviving replicas detect the failure and elect AZ 2 using Multi-Paxos.

steps.title: Wait out the old lease
steps.text: The new leader serves no writes or consistent reads until the old leader's lease has expired, which takes a couple of seconds. That guarantees two leaders never serve at the same time. It's also why a false failure detection costs availability.

steps.title: Serving again
steps.text: AZ 2 accepts writes, with AZ 3 completing the quorum, while autoadmin replaces the failed replica. For planned deployments, leaders hand over voluntarily so nobody waits for a lease.
